story.headline: The dollar held near its highest since April 2025 overnight, keeping the yen just shy of 160 per dollar. UK third-quarter growth matched forecasts, leaving a December Bank of England hike an open question.

reads.policy: Bets on faster Federal Reserve rate rises held overnight, keeping the dollar near its highest since April 2025. Hikes from Europe, Britain and Japan are expected too but already priced, so the gap keeps widening in the dollar's favour. Strong Japanese wholesale prices firmed the case for a Bank of Japan hike in December.
reads.growth: UK growth matched forecasts in the third quarter, solid enough to back the Bank of England's November hike but not enough to settle December. The US economy still looks firmer than Australia's, Canada's or New Zealand's, a split that favours the dollar. Euro-area growth figures on Friday are the next read.
reads.inflation: US inflation is running at about twice the Fed's goal, which keeps the Fed hiking and supports the dollar. In Japan, the weak yen is pushing wholesale prices up fast, adding pressure on the Bank of Japan to raise rates. Oil's dip overnight eases the worry a little.
reads.risk: Markets stayed calm overnight, so the safe-haven franc and yen drew little support. Talk of direct US–Iran talks eased some Gulf fears. A sudden flare-up in the Gulf is still the main thing that could change the mood fast.
reads.tot: Oil gave back Wednesday's gains on reports that Vice President JD Vance may meet Iran's security chief. Cheaper oil helps energy buyers such as Japan and the euro area and takes some support from the Canadian dollar. Tanker attacks near Hormuz keep a floor under prices.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds lean toward the dollar and the yen and against the kiwi, the Canadian dollar and the euro. The dollar's rise has gone with most of those bets, though the large bet on the yen is losing money as it weakens. The next weekly report is due Friday.
reads.fiscal: Weak demand at US government bond sales this week pushed long-term borrowing costs up, as buyers asked for more pay to hold US debt. That supports the dollar for now but is a worry if it spreads. A 30-year bond sale on Thursday is the next check.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike. Hot October inflation has made a December hike close to certain, and talk of faster rises has kept the dollar near its highest since April 2025.
fed.priced: December: hike near certain, with a half-point move a growing minority bet; January: another hike more likely than not.
fed.why: US inflation is running at about twice the Fed's 2% goal and officials say it is spreading beyond energy. Governor Christopher Waller has raised a half-point step, and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan wants at least two more hikes.
fed.watch: US jobless claims Thursday, a speech by New York Fed President John Williams late Thursday, and US producer prices on Friday at 7:30 AM CT. The decision is December 9.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October and has said more hikes may be needed. Notes from that meeting showed a real debate but no new signal, and bets on a December hike sit at about one in three.
boc.priced: December: hold is the base case; hike about one in three.
boc.why: Dearer energy lifted Canadian inflation and the bank expects it to stay near 3% for over a year, but the job market keeps weakening. That gives it reasons to move slowly.
boc.watch: Oil prices, which fell overnight on talk of US–Iran talks, and Canadian inflation figures later this month. The decision is December 9.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a 4–3 vote, though members agreed more tightening is likely. Rising unemployment has cut bets on a December hike to below even.
rbnz.priced: December: hike less likely than not.
rbnz.why: Price pressures argue for a hike, but unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for patience.
rbnz.watch: Whether stocks stay calm, the official election result on November 27, and what the next government means for the budget, before the December 9 decision.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held its deposit rate at 2.50% in October, and markets expect a hike in December. Because that hike is already priced, it gives the euro little support while US rate bets keep rising.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the goal, mostly because of energy, but shoppers are cutting back and borrowing costs have already risen. That makes the bank wary of doing too much.
ecb.watch: President Christine Lagarde speaks Thursday at 1:30 PM CT, and euro-area growth figures come Friday at 4:00 AM CT. The decision is December 17.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan holds at 1.25% but a December hike is likely, and faster-than-expected wholesale prices strengthened that case. With the dollar near 160 yen, the bank is under pressure to act.
boj.why: The weak yen is pushing up import costs, and wholesale prices rose 7.1% from a year earlier. Board member Kazuyuki Asada warned against hiking too soon, but markets still see December as likely.
boj.watch: Whether Japan steps in to buy yen near 160 per dollar, and speeches by Bank of Japan board members. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest since 2008, but three members wanted to wait. Weak consumer confidence and a slump in home lending since then support the case for a pause.
rba.priced: December: no firm pricing yet; the bank itself hinted at a pause.
rba.why: Inflation is still too high, but households are feeling the rate rises, with new home loans falling sharply, and the board is split. So the bank wants to see how its hikes work first.
rba.watch: Australian jobs figures for October next week, and the mood in global stock markets, before the December 8 decision.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5 and said more may follow while the Middle East conflict lasts. UK growth matched forecasts in the third quarter, which supports the pound but does not settle a second hike.
boe.priced: December: a second hike more likely than not.
boe.why: UK inflation is at its highest in about a year and the bank fears dear energy will keep it there. Growth held up after the hike, so there is no sign rates are choking the economy yet.
boe.watch: UK inflation figures for October, due later this month, and any steer from Bank of England officials. The decision is December 17.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and says it can still sell francs if they get too strong. Higher October inflation has made another cut less likely, and markets mostly expect a hold in December.
snb.why: Inflation is low and a strong franc keeps import prices down, so the bank has no reason to hike. October's rise in inflation makes a cut less pressing.
snb.watch: How far the franc moves as war fears ease, and the mood in stock markets, before the December 10 decision.

USD.summary: The dollar sits in the middle of the board: rate and inflation support are partly offset by a Democratic Congress. Bets on faster Fed hikes have kept it near its highest since April 2025.

notes.policy: A December Fed hike looks close to certain, and several officials now talk of moving faster, even by half a point.
notes.inflation: US core inflation has run at about twice the Fed's goal for three months, which keeps pressure on it to raise rates.
notes.fiscal: With Democrats controlling Congress, President Trump's spending plans look harder to pass, which trims some support for the dollar.

EUR.summary: The euro sits near the bottom of the board: weak growth, dear energy and France's debt worries outweigh an expected December rate hike. It fell to its lowest since May 2025 as bets on faster Fed hikes lifted the dollar.

notes.policy: A December European Central Bank hike is expected, but euro rates still sit below US and UK rates, so the gap works against the euro.
notes.growth: Business surveys and shoppers in the euro area have weakened, with France's economy shrinking again.
notes.inflation: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal, which keeps a December hike on the table.
notes.tot: The euro area buys most of its energy abroad, so dear oil drains money out of the region, though the recent fall in prices eases that.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold one of their biggest bets against the euro in years, so good news could set off a sharp rebound as they close it.
notes.fiscal: France's high debt and shaky budget keep investors demanding extra pay to hold French bonds, which weighs on the euro.

GBP.summary: The pound sits near the top of the board after the Bank of England raised rates to 4.00% and signalled more may follow. UK growth matched forecasts in the third quarter, but a faster Fed has trimmed the pound's edge.

notes.policy: The Bank of England hiked in November, and its governor said it is unlikely to be the last while the Middle East conflict lasts.
notes.growth: UK growth matched forecasts in the third quarter and business surveys are the strongest since February, even though shoppers have pulled back.
notes.inflation: UK inflation is at its highest in about a year, keeping pressure on the Bank of England.

JPY.summary: The yen sits low on the board because Japanese rates are far below others and Japan pays dearly for imported energy. A likely December rate hike helps a little, but the dollar is close to 160 yen.

notes.policy: At 1.25%, the Bank of Japan's rate is far below other major banks, though fast-rising wholesale prices make a December hike likely.
notes.risk: The yen tends to gain when stock markets get scared, as they did in early November, and loses some of that pull when they calm.
notes.tot: Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so dear oil weighs on the yen, though the recent fall in prices eases that.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold one of their biggest bets on the yen in years, and those bets lose money as the yen weakens, which could make them close fast.

CHF.summary: The franc sits in the middle of the board: its safe-haven pull is offset by inflation too low to need higher rates. The Swiss National Bank also says it can sell francs if they get too strong.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is low, so the central bank has no need to raise rates from zero.
notes.risk: The franc draws money when markets get nervous, but with stocks rising it has had little of that support lately.

AUD.summary: The Aussie scores well on the board thanks to the highest rates among the major central banks and firm commodity prices. It still trades mostly on stock-market mood and US rates, and slowing at home argues for a pause.

notes.policy: Australia's interest rate is the highest among the major central banks, though the governor hinted at a pause.
notes.growth: Australian unemployment is at a five-year high and home lending has slumped, though China's stronger buying helps exporters.
notes.inflation: Inflation is running above the Reserve Bank of Australia's forecasts, which kept it hiking.
notes.tot: Australia sells commodities abroad, and firm prices support its earnings.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the Aussie, so better news could set off a sharp rebound as they close those bets.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits mid-board: the Bank of Canada's October hike and oil exports help, but job losses have cut bets on more hikes. Oil's dip on talk of US–Iran talks has weighed on it.

notes.policy: The Bank of Canada raised rates in October and says more may be needed, though its meeting notes added no new signal and markets doubt a December move.
notes.growth: Canada lost jobs in September and October, and growth has stalled.
notes.inflation: Rising costs for Canadian producers point to more inflation ahead.
notes.tot: Canada exports oil, so prices still well above last year support its earnings, though the slide from October's highs trims that help.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits low on the board because rising unemployment has cut bets on a December rate hike. Bets on faster Fed hikes keep the US dollar firm against it.

notes.growth: New Zealand's unemployment rose to its highest since 2015.
notes.tot: Firm prices for dairy, New Zealand's main export, and stronger Chinese buying support its earnings.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the kiwi, so better news could set off a sharp rebound as they close those bets.
